Project Name: Evil Eye on Mars

Tagline: Earth’s evil-eye bead, Lake Meke, watching over Martian life

Evil Eye on Mars is an interactive 3D map that helps astronauts choose where to land and explore on Mars. It layers NASA data (MOLA, CRISM, HiRISE) and scores each site on Terra (landing and navigation safety) and Vita (astrobiological potential). Vita is anchored to Lake Meke, Türkiye’s salty crater lake known as “Earth’s evil-eye bead”, our Earth reference for Martian biosignatures.
summary: Evil Eye on Mars is an interactive 3D decision-support tool that helps mission planners balance landing safety and astrobiological potential across 16 Martian sites, using Lake Meke in Konya, Türkiye as an Earth analog.   Every Mars landing site involves a trade-off: none of the 16 candidates scores 100/100 on both criteria, ranging from safe but biologically poor Hellas Planitia (99 safety, 30 life) to risky, lake-bearing Melas Chasma (39 safety, 73 life).   Built with NASA MGS MOLA, Viking MDIM 2.1, and Landsat 5/8 data plus 119 cited sources, our tool evaluates sites using three transparent scores:   Terra (Safety): Evaluates MOLA slope, rock abundance, and elevation, applying an engineering No-Go filter above 20° slope.   Vita (Life Potential): Assesses five biosignature criteria independently scored by a geologist and biologist (rho = 0.86 agreement).   Meke Match (Earth Analog): Compares six orbital and mineralogical features against Lake Meke—a drying volcanic salt maar (pH 6.58–8.25, halophiles up to 25% NaCl)—displaying unknowns as explicit uncertainty ranges rather than guesses.   Users adjust live priority sliders or mission presets to update rankings and the Pareto front. Under balanced weighting, Oxia Planum ranks first (86.5), while Gale (90–100%) and Jezero (75–100%) show the strongest confirmed match to Lake Meke.
details:
What It Does & How It Works Evil Eye on Mars is an interactive 3D decision-support web application that helps mission planners evaluate and rank 16 Martian landing candidates by balancing engineering safety against astrobiological life potential. Users can adjust independent priority sliders or switch between preset mission profiles (Balanced, Safety First, Search for Life, and Crewed Mission) to inspect real-time rankings, Pareto-optimal sites, and telemetry breakdowns.

For every site, the decision engine calculates three transparent metrics: 1. Terra Score (Landing Safety): Evaluates elevation, regional slope, and rock abundance using NASA MGS MOLA data, automatically applying an engineering No-Go filter if the steepest 10% of regional slopes exceeds 20° (the Mars Science Laboratory limit).

2. Vita Score (Life Potential): Assesses five astrobiological preservation criteria (rock age, water duration, biosignature minerals, sediment and burial, and radiation shielding), independently scored on a 0–3 scale by our team's geologist and biologist with strong inter-rater agreement (Spearman's rho = 0.86).

3. Meke Match (Earth Analog): Compares each Martian site across six orbital and mineralogical features (chloride, crater lake morphology, paleolake history, sulfates, volcanic origin, and pH) against Lake Meke in Konya, Türkiye. Rather than treating unknown parameters as zero, the system outputs an explicit uncertainty range and flags sites with less than 50% data coverage as having insufficient data.

Creativity & Earth Analog Innovation
Nicknamed "the evil eye of the world," Lake Meke is a hypersaline volcanic maar (1.17 km wide, 276 m deep, pH 6.58–8.25, chloride-dominated, hosting halophilic microorganisms at up to 25% NaCl) that has progressively dried into a salt flat between 1990 and 2024. By pairing multi-decadal NASA/USGS Landsat time-series imagery with peer-reviewed geochemical and microbiological literature, our project bridges terrestrial extreme-environment science with planetary mission planning.

Factors Considered & Scientific Rigor
Our multidisciplinary team (information management, software engineering, geology, and biology) integrated 119 cited scientific sources and validated the scoring model with over 35 automated tests against manual calculations. Under balanced 50/50 weighting, Oxia Planum ranks first overall (86.5), while Gale Crater (90–100%) and Jezero Crater (75–100%) demonstrate the strongest confirmed analog similarity to Lake Meke. We also explicitly document methodological limits, including regional MOLA pixel resolution (~3.7 km) and the difference between terrestrial NaCl brines and Martian Mg-sulfate brines.

Tools, Languages & NASA Data Used
- Frontend & Visualization: React, TypeScript, Vite, and an interactive 3D Mars globe interface with bilingual (English/Turkish) support.
- Deployment & Open Source: Hosted on Vercel with source code and full bibliography (REFERENCES.md) published on GitHub under the MIT License.
- Open NASA/USGS Datasets: MGS MOLA MEGDR elevation (NASA PDS), Viking MDIM 2.1 global mosaic (NASA/USGS), and Landsat 5 & 8 multispectral imagery (NASA/USGS).

Benefits & Intended Impact
No single Martian site scores 100/100 on both safety and science—ranging from safe but biologically poor Hellas Planitia (99 safety, 30 life) to risky, lake-bearing Melas Chasma (39 safety, 73 life). Evil Eye on Mars gives engineers and astrobiologists a shared, transparent platform to visualize trade-offs, trace every score back to cited literature, and communicate complex planetary science through a relatable Earth analog.

Live App: https://evil-eye-on-mars.vercel.app
Source Code & 119 References: https://github.com/aysgulkryl/Evil-Eye-on-Mars
